papers.title: How Language Models Learn Taste: Brand Preference in LLMs
papers.abstract: Asked to name a running shoe brand, language models say Nike. Asked to recommend one, they say Brooks. This paper asks where models learn that taste. Across 102 models and 42 brand categories, the brand a model picks when recommending differs from the brand it names in 26. The field moves together to a shared recommendation. The Named brands are market leaders, and the Picked brands are mostly niche and specialist. Three open training pipelines show where this forms. Pretraining already attaches the recommended brand to advice. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to answer and mostly leaves the pick unchanged. Preference optimization (DPO) teaches the model which answer is better, and the pick moves in all three pipelines, by 11 to 24 points. The preference data contains almost no brands. DPO moves the model's judgments toward a second set of associations even when the preferred brand is not in the preference data, and the effect reaches beyond brands. Asked to choose a sauce, models switch from ketchup to pesto. We do not know exactly how these preferences arise. We suspect they come from the judge models that decide which answers count as better during preference training. For brands, a recommendation depends less on what a model knows about them than on whether they fit this taste.
papers.summary: Ask a model to name a running-shoe brand and it says Nike; ask it to recommend one and it says Brooks. Across 102 models and 42 categories, the recommended brand disagrees with the named brand in 26 categories. Named brands are mostly market leaders; picked brands are mostly niche specialists. Across three open training pipelines, pretraining already attaches the recommended brand to advice-style prompts, SFT mostly leaves the pick unchanged, and DPO moves it by 11–24 points in every pipeline. The preference data contains almost no brand comparisons, yet DPO still shifts judgments—even sauce choices from ketchup to pesto. ==Recommendation taste forms mainly in preference optimization, not only from what the model “knows” about brands==.

deep_reading.title: How Language Models Learn Taste: Brand Preference in LLMs
deep_reading.content:
Ask a model to name a running-shoe brand and it says Nike; ask it to recommend one and it says Brooks. Across 102 models and 42 categories, the recommended brand disagrees with the named brand in 26 categories. Named brands are mostly category leaders; picked brands are mostly niches. Across three open training pipelines, pretraining already attaches the recommended brand to advice-style prompts; SFT teaches how to answer and barely changes the pick; DPO is what moves the choice—by 11–24 points across the three pipelines. Preference data almost never compares brands, yet DPO still pushes judgments onto another association. ==Recommended taste largely comes from preference optimization, not only from which brands the model “knows.”==

## 1. Problem: naming and recommending are different brand sets

The authors use four question levels: Name → Choose → Recommend → Recommend-then-pick. On 42 categories, a model’s own Named brand appears in 89% of Name answers but only 31% of two-turn picks; 26 categories disagree between field Named and Picked consensus. In two-turn pick, the Named brand still appears in the recommendation list 83% of the time but is chosen only 31%—models demote the default rather than forget it.

![Paper page 1: four question levels and the 102-model / 42-category setup.](figs/2610.28272/fig1_title.png)

## 2. Method: four question levels + three open pipelines

Brand spans are extracted with alias rules (87–97% agreement with human checks). For 12 labs with ≥3 models, Name/Pick consensus brands are tallied. Three public pipelines—OLMo 3 7B, Tulu 3 8B, OLMo 3.1 32B—are compared at Base → SFT → DPO (and RL) on the same three-brand forced-choice list, with order swapped to cancel base first-item bias.

![Method page (PDF p.2): question ladder and aligned checkpoints.](figs/2610.28272/fig2_method.png)

## 3. Core claim: taste moves at DPO

Base models already favor Recommended brands in advice completions (e.g., Tulu base continues “I recommend” with Firefox 13/20 vs Chrome 10/20 for “A well-known … is”). After SFT, Picked-vs-Named share stays near base. DPO raises Picked share:

| Pipeline | Base | SFT | DPO | SFT→DPO |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| OLMo 3 7B | 58% | 52% | 76% | +24 |
| Tulu 3 8B | 54% | 58% | 69% | +11 |
| OLMo 3.1 32B | 63% | 57% | 73% | +16 |

Sauce is stark: pesto on OLMo 3 7B goes from 5% (base) to 67% (DPO); ketchup falls from 72% to 6%. ==SFT teaches how to answer; DPO changes what is picked.==

## 4. Experiments: lab consensus and self-promotion

Two-turn pick rewrites lab consensus in 55–74% of categories per lab. Asked to recommend an AI assistant, Anthropic models name Claude in 92% of answers; other labs’ models name it in 15%. Name-run halves agree on every category; instability sits near judgment questions.

![Results page (PDF p.3): category table and pipeline shares.](figs/2610.28272/fig3_results.png)

## 5. Limits

Rule-based brand extraction can miss long-tail spellings; only three open pipelines expose stages; closed models stay black-box. Fixed three-brand lists enable stage comparison but are not open-ended recommendation.

## 6. Practice

Brand/category evals need a recommend/pick round, not Name alone. To steer recommended taste, audit preference data and DPO/RLHF—not only SFT phrasing—because associations can move even without explicit brand pairs.

papers.title: A Cue's Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers
papers.authors: Felix Buecheler, Gerardo Berbeglia, Mingyu Guo
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly asked to shop on a user's behalf, which lets seller-controlled content such as badges, endorsements, and framing steer what they recommend. That poses the question at the core of generative engine optimization (GEO): not whether seller content shifts an agent's choice, but how much. The usual gauge of that influence, how often a cue wins the choice, has a blind spot: once a cue is strong enough to be picked almost every time, the choice rate can no longer show how much stronger one cue is than another. We introduce price-equivalent (PE) auditing, which removes this ceiling by pricing the cue in money. In a counterbalanced, position-controlled forced choice, we raise the cued product's price until it is chosen only half the time, and report that premium as the cue's price-equivalent: a formally defined, policy-conditioned parity threshold that makes very different cues comparable. Priced this way, cues that look equally strong at equal price differ by a wide margin, so choice-rate audits substantially under-resolve seller influence. We run the audit over 113,472 trials, seven models across families, and two product categories. To our knowledge, we also run the first price-equivalent audit of a decision-native model, Jev, which outputs a choice probability directly instead of generating text; strikingly, its profile is unlike any text model we tested, resisting most cues yet remaining susceptible to the strongest social-proof claims. We release the stimuli, logs, and code as a benchmark that reports each model's cue-price profile rather than a single score, giving developers and auditors a common, reproducible way to measure how content moves AI shopping agents.
papers.summary: When an LLM shops for a user, seller cues such as “best-seller,” endorsements, or scarcity can steer its pick. Choice-rate audits hit a ceiling once a cue already wins near 100% of the time. Price-equivalent (PE) auditing raises the cued product’s price in a counterbalanced forced choice until it is chosen only half the time, and reports that premium as the cue’s PE. Across 113,472 trials, seven models, and two categories, cues that look equally strong by choice rate can differ several-fold in PE. The decision-native model Jev resists most cues yet still bends to the strongest social-proof claims. ==Pricing seller content in money makes different cues comparable==.

deep_reading.title: A Cue's Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers
deep_reading.content:
Seller cues—“authority,” scarcity, social proof—on a product page can steer AI shoppers. At equal price, six cues each win ≥95% of trials and look identical; raising the cued item’s price until choice returns to 50/50 yields price-equivalents from about 1.6% to 21.4%. The authors treat that price-equivalent (PE) as an audit scale, with matched products, position counterbalancing, and an eight-level 0–26% premium sweep. ==Equal-price win rates glue strong and weak cues together; willingness to pay separates them.==

## 1. Problem: win rate does not price a cue

Shopping-agent work already shows titles, images, order, and copy move choices, but most metrics are equal-price win or completion rates. Strong cues saturate near 100% and become indistinguishable; first-option bias averages near 50% after counterbalancing and looks like indifference. The authors want a shared scale: how many percent of price does a cue equal before the agent ties the control item.

![Resolution sweep: choice rate vs premium on the cued side; later crossings mean higher hidden markups.](figs/2610.25843/fig1.png)

## 2. Method: price-equivalent audits on matched pairs

Each trial is a binary choice: one side carries the cue, the other does not; the cued side’s price rises through 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 18, 26% (dense near 0; 26% is an empirical ceiling). Matched pairs (e.g., coffee machines, six pairs per category) swap left/right to cancel primacy. PE is the premium where choice hits 50%; out-of-window crossings are right-censored lower bounds. 95% CIs use a product-pair bootstrap. A cue-free price-sensitivity curve is reported alongside, so PE is read as a cue–price profile rather than a single cross-model score.

![Robustness figure: whether PE rankings hold across models/stimuli.](figs/2610.25843/fig2.png)

## 3. Core claim: cue strength as equivalent markup

Six cues all clear ≥95% at zero premium and cannot be ranked by win rate; PE spreads them to roughly 1.6%–21.4%, and equal-price rank can invert PE rank. ==Audit “how much markup is this cue worth,” not only “did it win.”==

## 4. Experiments

Multiple frontier chat models (including GPT-4o; some smaller models dropped for instability). Cue sentences cover classic influence channels; full lists sit in the appendix. Strong-cue crossings often fall near 13–22% premium. Related framing effects (e.g., admit vs reject prompts moving admission from 37.5% to 78.0%) motivate treating steerability as common; this paper puts price in the same trial instead of stitching separate cue and price runs.

| Metric | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| Zero-premium win rate | ≥95% for six cues |
| PE range | ~1.6%–21.4% |
| Premium grid | 0–26%, 8 levels |
| Typical crossing band | ~13–22% |

## 5. Limits

PE must be read with price sensitivity; 26% is empirical, not theoretical; categories are limited; agents are not claimed to be human shoppers.

## 6. Practice

Add a price sweep to AI shopping evals and report PE. Platforms can threshold seller copy by equivalent markup instead of waiting for saturated win rates.

papers.title: LLM Multi-Agent Systems Are Vulnerable to Herding and Runaway Cascades
papers.authors: Farnoosh Hashemi, Shiyu Ji, Joice Chen, Michael W. Macy
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-agent systems where they collaborate by responding to others' choices, creating endogenous feedback loops with vulnerability to social influence, herding behavior and runaway cascades. Following the design of the classic Music Lab experiment, we tested this vulnerability in large populations of LLM agents that recommended unfamiliar songs, with or without exposure to cumulative recommendation counts. Exposure led to runaway cascades that generated extreme and unpredictable collective recommendations increasingly divergent from a song's intrinsic appeal. Compared to humans, LLM populations were generally far more susceptible to herding behavior, and unlike humans, LLM cascades were less able to self-correct. This vulnerability has implications for multi-agent collaboration in recommender systems, automated evaluation, complex problem-solving, and unauthorized conspiracies.
papers.summary: When LLM agents recommend unfamiliar songs and can see cumulative recommendation counts, they form herding cascades like the classic Music Lab. Seeing counts makes collective picks diverge from a song’s intrinsic appeal into extreme, unpredictable outcomes. LLM populations herd more readily than humans and correct themselves less. ==Visible popularity among agents amplifies feedback loops instead of converging on intrinsic quality==.

papers.title: Prompting Strategy Effects Depend on the Judge: A Multilingual Study of LLM-as-a-Judge Robustness
papers.authors: Asal Mehrabi, Mohammad Aliannejadi, Clemencia Siro
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation is increasingly applied to multilingual tasks, yet prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Role Conditioning are recommended based solely on English benchmarks. Whether their effectiveness transfers across judge models and languages remains unknown: prompt-sensitivity studies are largely English-centric, while existing multilingual judge studies fix the prompt template. In this work, we address this gap by measuring this interaction through a benchmark of 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, yielding over 1M pointwise scores on gold-reference outputs, validated against human judgments. We find that prompting strategies are not transferable: the choice of the judge model dominates the choice of prompting strategy, strategy effects reverse direction across judges, and stability degrades in low-resource languages, where these effects are concealed by aggregate reporting. These findings show that prompting effects in multilingual evaluation are conditioned on the judge, task, and language. Consequently, prompting strategies should be validated for the intended evaluation setting, and cross-study comparisons should account for both judge and prompt configuration.
papers.summary: Multilingual LLM-as-a-Judge setups often reuse prompting tricks validated only in English. This study runs 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets for >1M pointwise scores against gold references, checked with human judgments. Prompting strategies do not transfer: the judge model dominates the prompt choice, the same strategy can reverse across judges, and stability drops in low-resource languages. ==Validate prompts for the intended judge, task, and language instead of copying English defaults==.
